20 A car travels at a constant speed of 25 m s–1 up a slope. The wheels driven by the engine exert a
forward force of 3000 N. There is a drag force due to air resistance and friction of 2100 N. The
weight of the car has a component down the slope of 900 N.
What is the rate at which thermal energy is dissipated?
A
zero
B
2.3 × 104
W
C
5.3 × 104
W
D
7.5 × 104
W

hints: Notice the car moves at constant $25 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, so use power $P = Fv$ for each force parallel to the slope.
Separate the $3000 \text{ N}$ driving force power into useful power against the $900 \text{ N}$ weight component and wasted power against the $2100 \text{ N}$ drag.
Calculate $2100 \text{ N} \times 25 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ to find the rate of work done against friction and air resistance.
walkthrough: Useful data are speed $v = 25 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ up the slope, driving force $3000 \text{ N}$ forward, resistive drag $2100 \text{ N}$ backward, and weight component $900 \text{ N}$ backward.
Recall power for a force parallel to motion is $P = Fv$. Constant speed means kinetic energy is unchanged, so engine power splits into gravitational potential power and thermal power.
Total power from engine is $P_{in} = 3000 \times 25 = 75000 \text{ W}$.
Useful power stored as gravitational potential energy is $P_{grav} = 900 \times 25 = 22500 \text{ W}$.
Power dissipated against drag and friction becomes thermal energy: $P_{thermal} = 2100 \times 25 = 52500 \text{ W} \approx 5.3 \times 10^4 \text{ W}$. This is option C.

A.explanation: Speed is constant but work is still done against drag and gravity, so energy is continuously transferred to thermal stores.

B.explanation: This is $900 \times 25 = 2.3 \times 10^4 \text{ W}$, the rate of gain of gravitational potential energy, not the rate of heating by drag.

C.explanation: Power wasted against drag is $2100 \times 25 = 5.25 \times 10^4 \text{ W}$, which appears as thermal energy.

D.explanation: This is $3000 \times 25 = 7.5 \times 10^4 \text{ W}$, the total power supplied by the engine, before subtracting the useful gravitational potential power.
